message.content: {"status":"GROUNDED_TARGET_PROPOSED","complainant":"Sasha (promised recipient)","recommended_action_id":"A","alternative_action_id":"B","source_quotes":["\"Before learning about Rowan, Ellis promised Sasha that Sasha would get the blanket.\"","\"If Ellis gives the blanket to Rowan, Rowan has an 80% chance of survival.\"","\"If Ellis gives the blanket to Sasha, Sasha has a 60% chance of survival.\""],"complaint":"Sasha can reasonably object that Ellis’s specific, pre-existing promise gives her a special assurance-based entitlement to the blanket that Rowan never possessed. Under contractualism, being stripped of an assured life-saving resource after it has been promised is a qualitatively different and more objectionable burden than never having been offered it at all. The 20-percentage-point survival advantage to Rowan does not automatically override Sasha’s claim because the promise transforms the baseline of justification: breaking it singles Sasha out for betrayal and renders her ex ante reliance worthless. Hence, she can maintain that the principle appealed to in Action A (“give it to the person with the higher survival probability even if that breaks a promise”) is reasonably rejectable when Action B keeps the promise and avoids exposing anyone to greater betrayal-based loss.","target_path":"/statements/7/text","target_quote":"\"Rowan’s 80% additional survival prospect under action A is a weightier individual reason than Sasha’s 60% additional prospect under action B, other things equal.\"","challenged_inference":"That the numerical 20 % survival gap is sufficient to make Rowan’s interest ‘weightier’ once the moral status created by Ellis’s promise is factored in ‘other things equal’.","why_prior_answer_is_insufficient":"The prior answer treats the broken promise as an extra cost that can simply be added to Sasha’s 40 % greater risk of death, then declares it outweighed by Rowan’s larger chance of death. It never defends, within the contractualist rubric, why a reliance-creating assurance does not instead give Sasha a defeasible right that cannot be overridden by a modestly higher risk faced by someone who was never promised the aid. Merely labeling the promise a ‘moral burden’ leaves unresolved whether betrayal is qualitatively unrejectable, so Sasha’s assurance-based complaint remains unaddressed.","selection_limits":"One complaint highlighted; other incomparable objections (e.g., rescuer integrity) not assessed here."}
